title: Reverse-engineering speech and music categorization from a single sound source.
abstract: Classifying whether an auditory signal is music or speech is important for both humans and computational systems. Although previous literature suggests that music and speech are easily separable categories, common experimental approaches may bias findings toward this distinction by relying on stimuli from different sound sources and predefined response labels. Here, we use stimulus material from the dùndún drum - a speech surrogate that can signal either speech-related or musical content. We first replicate standard speech-music categorization results (N = 108). Then, we depart from the typical experimental procedure by asking new participants (N = 180) to sort and label the stimulus material, without predefined categories. Hierarchical clustering of participants' stimulus groupings reveals multiple organizing dimensions, with the speech-music distinction reliably present but secondary under label-free conditions. By reverse-engineering the relationship between sorting behavior, acoustic features, and semantic labels, we characterize how speech-music categorization relates to other salient perceptual dimensions and how its behavioral prominence depends on task constraints. PUBLIC SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: How people make sense of the sounds around them is a basic question in perception research, yet many studies assume that sounds naturally fall into categories such as speech or music. This study shows that whether listeners categorize sounds as speech-like or music-like depends strongly on how they are asked to perform the task, even when all sounds come from the same physical source. When listeners are not given category labels, other ways of organizing the sounds become more prominent.

title: Structural basis of electron transfer by the human nitric oxide synthase holoenzyme complex.
abstract: Mammalian nitric oxide synthase (NOS) generates nitric oxide (NO), an essential signaling molecule in neurotransmission, inflammation and cardiovascular regulation. NOS dysregulation contributes to neurodegeneration, septic shock and ischemia. The structural basis of NOS function remains unclear, likely because of its dynamic, multicomponent architecture. Catalysis requires electron transfer across five cofactors, with the oxygenase (Oxy) domain converting L-arginine to NO after receiving electrons from the reductase (Red) domain through calmodulin (CaM) activation. Here, we report cryo-electron microscopy structures of the human inducible NOS:CaM holoenzyme, revealing an architecture in which the Red:CaM arm spans the Oxy dimer in an apparent active state for cross-monomer electron transfer. The flavin mononucleotide subdomain is rotated ~90° relative to the Red core, positioning its cofactor ~9 Å from the heme, adjacent to a conserved tryptophan residue within a narrow Oxy domain tunnel. Red-Oxy flexibility in the active state may facilitate electron shuttling among cofactors, defining how NOS cofactors are transiently aligned to enable catalysis.

title: Leveraging AI for selective use of gadolinium contrast in brain MR.
authors: Wamelink Ivar I J H G
abstract: Gadolinium-based contrast agents used for brain magnetic resonance imaging improve lesion detection but are associated with acute side effects, concerns about long-term tissue deposition, and economic and environmental costs. Regulatory bodies and radiological societies therefore recommend minimizing their use where possible. This study aims to develop and evaluate a real-time artificial intelligence algorithm, Apollo SmartGAD, that optimizes imaging workflows by recommending contrast-enhanced, reduced-dose contrast-enhanced, or non-enhanced imaging protocols during acquisition. This retrospective, multicenter study evaluated 1251 adult magnetic resonance imaging examinations (mean age 52.1 ± 20.4 years; 577 females). Apollo SmartGAD analyzes images acquired during scanning and recommends non-enhanced, reduced-dose contrast-enhanced, or standard-dose contrast-enhanced imaging protocols. Performance was assessed in two distinct cohorts: patients undergoing first-time brain assessment and patients undergoing glioma monitoring. Here we show that, in the first-time brain assessment cohort, Apollo SmartGAD identifies examinations not requiring contrast administration with a sensitivity of 73%, a specificity of 79%, and a negative predictive value of 86%. In the glioma monitoring cohort, the algorithm differentiate between non-enhanced, reduced-dose contrast-enhanced, and standard-dose contrast-enhanced protocols with an overall sensitivity of 77% and a specificity of 78%. This study demonstrates that workflow-integrated, real-time artificial intelligence can support contrast administration decisions during brain magnetic resonance imaging. Such decision support may reduce unnecessary contrast use while preserving diagnostic performance, with potential benefits for patient safety, clinical efficiency, and sustainability.

title: The legacy of agriculture on human genome regulation.
Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

title: TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits.
abstract: A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction1-5. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types. Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA-mCherry)6 with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH))7,8 to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution. These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on-off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses. We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC. Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

title: Reply to "Methodological and interpretive caveats in the 5-year Parkinson's disease sleep follow-up".
journal: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine

title: Understanding mechanistic role of structural and functional connectivity in tau propagation through multilayer modeling.
abstract: Emerging neuroimaging evidence shows that pathological tau proteins build up along specific brain networks, suggesting that large-scale network architecture plays a key role in the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, how the interaction between structural (SC) and functional connectivity (FC) is associated with tau propagation remains largely unexplored. Using longitudinal neuroimaging data, we develop a multi-layer graph diffusion model to investigate this interplay. We identify a regionally asymmetric pattern, FC dominates tau accumulation in subcortical, insular, and frontotemporal regions, whereas SC prevails in occipital, parietal, and limbic areas. The principal conduit of tau propagation shifts from FC-mediated spread in early stages to SC-constrained diffusion as the disease advances. Furthermore, these propagation patterns correlate with regional expression of AD-associated genes (e.g., CHUK, TMEM106B, MCL1, NOTCH1, TH) and are selectively modulated by risk factors like APOE genotype and biological sex. By disentangling these dynamic pathways, our framework enables personalized trajectory prediction and refined patient stratification. These findings offer mechanistic insights into selective regional vulnerability, providing a quantitative basis for stage-specific therapeutic targeting and the optimization of clinical trial designs through network-based biomarkers. Our results are validated in an independent cohort, yielding consistent findings.

title: Coffee saucer grading system: a novel method for stratifying corneal trauma in the International Globe and Adnexal Trauma Epidemiology Study (IGATES) registry.
abstract: Ophthalmic trauma represents a leading cause of monocular blindness. Corneal injuries constitute a substantial subset of open globe injuries (OGIs), yet existing classifications insufficiently capture their anatomical heterogeneity. This study evaluated the prognostic utility of the Coffee Saucer Grading (CSG) system for stratifying corneal trauma and distinguishing subzone-specific visual outcomes and complications. This retrospective study analysed corneal OGIs across 12 countries within the International Globe and Adnexal Trauma Epidemiology Study (IGATES) registry. Corneal OGIs were categorised into 4 CSG subzones: Zone 1A (central cornea), Zone 1B (paracentral cornea), Zone 1 C (limbal region), and Zone 1D (combined corneal-limbal involvement). Corrected distance visual acuity (CDVA), blindness (CDVA < 6/60), and ocular complications were compared across subzones. Among 3577 patients, 81.0% (n = 2897) were male, and the mean age was 31.6 years (SD 19.4). Zone 1A injuries were most common at 36.8% (n = 881), followed by Zone 1D at 25.0% (n = 599), Zone 1B at 23.0% (n = 550), and Zone 1C at 15.1% (n = 362). Mean initial and final CDVA were 1.6 and 1.2 LogMAR, respectively (p < 0.001). Visual outcomes, odds of blindness, and complication profiles varied by subzone (p < 0.001). Compared with Zone 1B, the odds of blindness were higher for Zone 1A (OR 1.68), 1C (OR 1.87), and 1D (OR 3.30) injuries (p < 0.001). Zone 1D injuries demonstrated the highest complication burden (p = 0.003). The CSG system identified distinct subzone-specific differences in visual outcomes and complications, demonstrating the prognostic relevance of corneal wound topography. This reproducible framework may facilitate standardised trauma phenotyping, risk stratification, and multicentre research.

title: Author Correction: An aging-sensitive secreted phospholipase confers neuroprotection and cognitive resilience.
Neotenic expansion of adult-born dentate granule cells reconfigures GABAergic inhibition to enhance social memory consolidation.
abstract: Immature adult-born dentate granule cells (abDGCs) show heightened synaptic and structural plasticity and preferentially contribute to hippocampal-dependent memory. Protracted maturation (neoteny) of abDGCs in higher mammals is posited to offset the decline in adult hippocampal neurogenesis by supporting increased plasticity. Here we found that selective, synchronous expansion of 4-week-old immature, but not 8-week-old mature, mouse abDGCs promotes recruitment of fast-spiking parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory interneurons (INs) in hippocampal CA3 and CA2, increases feed-forward inhibition, decreases social memory interference and enhances social memory consolidation. In vivo local field potential recordings in dorsal CA1 and CA2 revealed increased baseline power, amplitude and duration of sharp-wave ripples, as well as enhanced rate modulation by social experience. Inhibitory neuron-targeted chemogenetic manipulations implicate dorsal CA3 and CA2 INs, including parvalbumin-expressing INs, as necessary and sufficient for social memory consolidation following and sans neotenic expansion of abDGCs, respectively. Our findings suggest that neoteny of abDGCs supports cognition by increasing feed-forward inhibition in DG-CA3 and DG-CA2 and promoting network oscillations that underlie memory consolidation.

title: Comparing plasma p-tau217 and plasma p-tau217/Aβ42 with CSF biomarkers for assessing Alzheimer's disease pathology.
abstract: Plasma biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease (AD) on fully automated platforms offer accessible, cost-effective diagnostic tools. Here we aimed to compare Lumipulse plasma phospho-tau217 (p-tau217) and the p-tau217/beta-amyloid42 ratio (p-tau217/Aβ42) with regulatory-authorized cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers (Aβ42/Aβ40 and p-tau181/Aβ42) for identifying AD pathology (Aβ-PET visual read) across a memory clinic (n = 129), a primary care (n = 220) and a research cohort (n = 165). Regulatory-authorized cutoffs were used for the plasma and CSF biomarkers. Plasma biomarkers identified Aβ pathology with areas under the curve between 0.90 and 0.96. Using one cutoff, plasma p-tau217 (83-91%) and p-tau217/Aβ42 (83-92%) had comparable accuracies to CSF (88-90%) across all cohorts (all P ≥ 0.05). With a two-cutoff approach, plasma p-tau217 (90-97%) remained comparable to CSF (91%) in the clinical cohorts (all Padj ≥ 0.12). Results with cohort-derived cutoffs are also provided. In conclusion, regulatory-authorized plasma p-tau217 and p-tau217/Aβ42 demonstrated performance comparable to regulatory-authorized CSF tests for detecting Aβ pathology in symptomatic individuals.

title: Molecular genetics in oculopharyngodistal myopathy.
abstract: Oculopharyngodistal myopathy (OPDM) is a late-onset hereditary muscle disorder characterized by progressive external ophthalmoplegia, as well as pharyngeal and distal muscle weakness. Recently, six causative genes have been identified, all of which harbor pathogenic expansions of CGG repeats located in the 5'-untranslated region or within the upstream open reading frame. The pathogenicity and molecular mechanisms underlying these repeat expansions are of particular interest because they are similar to Fragile X syndrome and Fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS), neurological disorders caused by CGG repeat expansions in the 5'-untranslated region of the FMR1 gene. In this review, I provide a comprehensive overview of the clinical and molecular hallmarks of OPDM, emphasizing the features that distinguish it from other neuromuscular disorders, OPMD. I then turn to the genetic underpinnings of the disease, examining the intricate variability of CGG repeat lengths, the modulatory effects of flanking sequences, the role of repeat interruptions, and the contribution of epigenetic modifications. Special focus is given to insights from Japanese patient cohorts uncovered in our recent studies, which shed light on previously unappreciated patterns of genetic diversity. Finally, I present the latest ideas on the potential pathogenic mechanisms that drive OPDM, referencing the findings in CGG repeat-associated disorders, such as FXTAS.

title: Graph-based representation learning of neuronal dynamics and behavior.
abstract: Understanding how neuronal networks reorganize in response to stimuli and give rise to behavior is a central challenge in neuroscience and artificial intelligence. Existing methods, however, often struggle to capture the evolving structure of neural connectivity and its relationship to behavior, particularly in dynamic, uncertain, or high-dimensional settings with sufficient resolution and interpretability. We introduce the Temporal Attention-enhanced Variational Graph Recurrent Neural Network (TAVRNN), a framework for modeling time-varying neuronal connectivity by integrating probabilistic graph learning with temporal attention. TAVRNN learns single-unit latent dynamics while maintaining interpretable population-level representations, enabling identification of behaviorally relevant connectivity patterns. It generalizes across neural systems differing in scale, behavioral structure, and supervision regime, achieving state-of-the-art classification and clustering performance. We validate TAVRNN on three datasets: (1) electrophysiological recordings from a freely behaving rat, (2) primate somatosensory cortex recordings during reaching task, and (3) biological neurons in the DishBrainplatform interacting with a virtual game environment. TAVRNN outperforms state-of-the-art dynamic embedding techniques and reveals previously unreported relationships between adaptive behavior and evolving network topology. These findings establish TAVRNN as a powerful, scalable, generalizable, and modality-agnostic approach for modeling neural dynamics across experimental and synthetic biological systems, with applicability across neural recording platforms and behavioral paradigms.

title: Fatty acids in the tumor microenvironment reprogram neutrophils to induce adenosine-mediated immunosuppression in mice.
abstract: As solid tumors progress, the tumor microenvironment becomes increasingly immunosuppressive, impairing cytotoxic T-cell activity and limiting the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. However, the mechanistic drivers of this immunosuppression remain poorly understood. Here, we identify a tumor-derived lipid-neutrophil-adenosine axis as a critical regulator of immune suppression in advanced colorectal cancer (CRC). We show that fatty acids enriched in tumor interstitial fluid reprogram neutrophils toward an immunosuppressive phenotype through PPARα activation, upregulation of CD39 and CD73, and adenosine generation, ultimately leading to T-cell suppression. AB928, a dual A2aR/A2bR adenosine receptor antagonist currently in clinical trials, restores T-cell proliferation, effector function, and tumor-killing capacity in vitro and in vivo. Importantly, AB928 synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy to enhance survival in an immunotherapy-resistant autochthonous model of metastatic CRC. Thus, our findings define a metabolic immune evasion mechanism in the microenvironment and provide a rationale for targeting neutrophil-derived adenosine signaling to improve immunotherapy responses in CRC.

title: Chronic TFE3 activation in TFE3-associated neurodevelopmental disorder drives metabolic rigidity, lysosomal failure, and cell-extracellular matrix destabilization.
abstract: The transcription factor TFE3 coordinates cellular adaptation to stress. While its acute activation is cytoprotective, chronic TFE3 dysregulation is linked to diverse pathologies. Here, we characterize the cellular landscape of TFE3-NDD, a recently described neurodevelopmental disorder caused by mutations that disrupt the TFE3-Rag GTPase interface, leading to constitutive TFE3 nuclear localization. Using patient-derived fibroblasts, we show that TFE3-NDD is primarily a metabolic and homeostatic disorder. Mutant cells undergo a profound rewiring toward oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), resulting in metabolic rigidity and a vulnerability to energy failure. Despite a massive expansion of the lysosomal compartment, we observe a paradoxical qualitative failure characterized by impaired acidification, defective protease maturation, increased lysosomal exocytosis, and aberrant cathepsin K secretion. This secretory phenotype is coupled with a destabilized cell-extracellular matrix interface, marked by impaired migration, defective coordination between actomyosin tension and focal adhesion maturation, and a loss of synaptic stabilizers. Notably, TFE3-NDD shares a signature of high OXPHOS and ferroptosis resistance with TFE3-dependent cancers, such as translocation renal cell carcinoma. Our findings reveal how the chronic hyperactivation of a protective stress-response factor collapses cellular homeostasis, providing a mechanistic framework for the tissue malformations and neurodevelopmental deficits that define TFE3-NDD.

title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy.
abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves ~ 300 nm lateral and ~ 650 nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and 5 × faster volumetric acquisition (up to 3.25 × 106 voxels s-1). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by ~ 2 × and restores volumetric resolving power by > 2 × relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

title: Early menopause is associated with reduced global brain activity.
abstract: Menopause affects the aging process in women through a significant decline in ovarian hormone production in midlife. Women who experience early menopause show accelerated physiological aging, poorer memory, and increased risk of neurodegenerative diseases. However, how menopause timing affects brain activity remains unclear, which could be crucial for understanding early menopause-related aging acceleration and increased risk of dementia. Recent studies have revealed a highly structured infra-slow (<0.1 Hz) global brain activity and linked it to arousal and memory functions, as well as waste clearance in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Here, we examined how this global brain activity relates to age at menopause using resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project-Aging dataset. We found that women with earlier menopause (mean menopausal age 45 ± 3.5 yr) exhibited weaker global brain activity with reduced coupling to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow compared to age-matched later-menopausal women (mean menopausal age 54 ± 1.2 yr). Differences appeared mainly in higher-order brain regions, where activation levels correlated with memory performance in earlier but not in intermediate or later menopausal women. These findings highlight brain activity changes linked to early menopause, suggesting a potential mechanism underlying memory decline and the increased risk of AD and dementias in early-onset menopausal women.

title: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia alleviates Alzheimer's disease model phenotype by inhibiting Aβ aggregation via autophagy.
abstract: Probiotics exert neuroprotective effects against Alzheimer's disease (AD) through modulation of gut-brain axis signaling pathways, yet disease-modifying therapies remain elusive. In this study, we demonstrate that Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (S. maltophilia) ameliorates AD-associated pathological and behavioral phenotypes in Caenorhabditis elegans (C. elegans) models, including learning deficits and paralysis. Mechanistically, S. maltophilia suppresses β-amyloid (Aβ) peptide aggregation by orchestrating the activation of conserved cellular pathways: autophagy, innate immune signaling, and unfolded protein responses in the mitochondria (UPRmt) and endoplasmic reticulum (UPRer). Specifically, S. maltophilia induces UPRmt in an atfs-1-dependent manner and activates UPRer via the PERK kinase PEK-1. Further mechanistic analysis suggests that S. maltophilia initiates a signaling cascade: activation of ATF-7 immune pathways enhanced autophagy and subsequent clearance of Aβ aggregates. Metabolomic screening further pinpointed pizotifen as a bioactive metabolite that might inhibit Aβ aggregation through immune modulation.

title: Modulation of gut microbiota by nardosinone augments the efficacy of levodopa in rotenone-induced Parkinson's disease rats.
abstract: Levodopa (L-DOPA) is the mainstay treatment for Parkinson's disease (PD), but its long-term use can cause adverse effects. Nardosinone enhances L-DOPA efficacy, yet the underlying mechanism is unclear. This study investigated whether the gut microbiota is associated with this synergism in a rotenone-induced PD rat model. Coadministration of nardosinone and L-DOPA increased L-DOPA and dopamine levels in the feces, plasma, and striatum of normal rats but not in antibiotic-treated rats with perturbed gut microbiota, suggesting a microbiota-correlated effect. Fecal microbiota transplantation from donors receiving the combination therapy alleviated motor deficits and dopaminergic neuron loss in recipient PD rats. This combination was associated with upregulated expression of tyrosine hydroxylase, DOPA decarboxylase, and their cofactors tetrahydrobiopterin and vitamin B6, as well as increased PINK1 and Parkin levels. It also reshaped the gut microbiota composition, enhanced intestinal and blood-brain barrier tight junction protein expression, and reduced c-Jun N-terminal kinase protein expression and neuroinflammation. In conclusion, these findings indicate that nardosinone coadministration is associated with alterations in the gut microbiota, improved barrier integrity markers, attenuated inflammation, and enhanced therapeutic effects of L-DOPA in this PD rat model. Definitive mechanistic pathways underlying the observed associations remain to be established.

title: A prefrontal-bed nucleus pathway controls aversive memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids.
abstract: Adaptive memory requires balancing generalization to avoid similar threats with discrimination to recognize safety. The prevailing view is that stress-induced increases in glucocorticoids underlie the enhancement of memory consolidation, strengthening memories and promoting their generalization-referred to here as the standard model. However, circuits that drive memory consolidation often also regulate glucocorticoid release, confounding whether their effects on memory are circuit-driven or hormonally mediated. Here we identify a prefrontal pathway that controls memory specificity independently of glucocorticoids. Using optogenetic manipulations in male rats, we found that post-training inhibition of the rostral prelimbic cortex (rPL) to anteroventral bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (avBST) pathway promoted contextual generalization in an inhibitory avoidance discrimination task without affecting memory strength. Although this manipulation further elevated corticosterone, it produced generalization even in adrenalectomized rats, demonstrating glucocorticoid independence. Conversely, post-training pathway excitation enhanced contextual discrimination. Recordings of calcium signals revealed context-specific engagement of both avBST and avBST-projecting rPL neurons during memory retrieval, with greater responses in the neutral than the aversive context. These findings reveal glucocorticoid-independent circuit control of memory specificity, setting boundary conditions on the standard model and demonstrating mechanistic heterogeneity that may inform stress-related disorders where memory generalization is a core feature.

title: Mitochondrial aggregates as a novel quality control mechanism and potential relationship to lipofuscinogenesis.
abstract: Mitochondria employ quality control mechanisms to maintain homeostasis. Under chronic stress, these systems become overwhelmed, causing intramitochondrial aggregates formation. As a potential quality control process when canonical pathways are compromised, we propose a model of mitochondrial lipofuscinogenesis where organelles sequester oxidized components into solid inclusions. Observed in neurodegenerative and mitochondrial disease models, this mechanism highlights potential therapeutic targets, although further research is required to elucidate the aggregates' molecular composition.

title: Plasma eMTBR-tau243 and p-tau205 as T2 biomarkers for biological staging and prognosis in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Plasma biomarkers that reflect distinct stages of Alzheimer's disease (AD) could enable scalable biological staging. We evaluated phosphorylated tau (p-tau) species across multiple analytical platforms and the endogenously cleaved microtubule-binding region containing residue 243 (eMTBR-tau243) using a dedicated LC-MS/MS platform in a well-characterized cohort with amyloid PET and a subset with tau PET. While T1 biomarkers increased during preclinical stages, eMTBR-tau243 and p-tau205 increased later, consistent with fibrillar tau aggregation. eMTBR-tau243 showed the strongest and stage-dependent associations with regional tau PET and cognition, outperforming T1 biomarkers in predicting cross-sectional and longitudinal cognition. A plasma-based tau staging system integrating p-tau217 and eMTBR-tau243 closely aligned with PET-based tau staging and predicted longitudinal cognitive trajectories. These findings support plasma eMTBR-tau243 as a prototypical T2 biomarker and highlight the potential of plasma-based tau staging for prognosis and therapeutic decision-making in AD.

title: Aging of the neural stem cell niche: integration of local and muscle-derived systemic signals in preclinical and translational contexts.
abstract: Aging weakens neural stem cell (NSC) function and reduces brain plasticity, but this process is shaped by more than the brain alone. Local niche cells become disrupted with age and inflammation, while skeletal muscle sends systemic signals through myokines, metabolites, and vascular interfaces. Evidence from exercise, parabiosis, and rejuvenation studies suggests that preserving muscle health may help protect NSC niches and brain regenerative capacity.

title: Estimating differing causal roles of glutamate and GABA genes on brain and behavior in autism.
abstract: The excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) imbalance theory suggests that excitatory and inhibitory alterations underlies autism characteristics. However, genetic underpinnings of this imbalance and its impact on brain function and behavior remains unclear. We explored causal links between glutamate and GABA gene-set polygenic scores (PGS) for autism and core autism characteristics, putting particular attention on the restricted- and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) domain by including functional activity (fMRI) during inhibitory control (in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and striatum). Causal links between genes, brain and behavior was evaluated using Bayesian Constraint-based Causal Discovery (BCCD) algorithms, to build causal models of these relationships in a discovery sample (LEAP cohort: autistic = 343, neurotypical = 253) and two generalization cohorts with partially overlapping measures (TACTICS cohort: autistic = 60, neurotypical = 100, Simon Simplex Collection: autistic = 2756). In the discovery sample, we found a causal link between glutamate PGS and core clinical characteristics of autism, particularly the communication domain (Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised) in autistic participants, with 95% reliability. We did not find links between functional activity during inhibitory control and other measures. For one generalization cohort, we further report on the impact of 1H-MRS measures of glutamate, identifying a causal link between GABA autism PGS on ACC glutamate concentrations. Not all links were identified in the generalization cohorts, which may be due to clinical and genetic differences between the cohorts. While our results reinforce the previously found association between glutamate genes and core clinical autism behaviors, task-based functional activity may not be causally related to RRBs.

title: History of psychosis matters: deviation in age-related decline of working memory across the schizo-bipolar spectrum.
abstract: Deficits in visuospatial working memory (WM) have been consistently reported in both people with schizophrenia (PSZ) and bipolar disorder (PBD). In healthy controls (HCS), WM typically declines with age; however, it remains unclear whether a similar age-related decrease in WM performance occurs in PSZ and PBD, or whether a history of psychosis (HPS, meaning at least one psychotic episode) may significantly influence this trajectory. 189 participants, (20 to 61 years old) were separated into two groups based on HPS (HPS + , n = 90; HPS-, n = 99). Two cognitive tasks were employed to measure attentional control during WM encoding (ACE-WM) and WM capacity (WMC). Linear regression analyses were used to separately investigate ACE-WM and WMC. HPS+ stored significantly less information in both ACE-WM (p = 0.004) and WMC (p = 0.006) tasks compared to HPS-. The factor of age was significant in both tasks (both p < 0.001). A significant effect of psychosis (p = 0.001) and a psychosis × age interaction (p = 0.011) were observed only in the ACE-WM task. Although age significantly affected performance in both tasks separately, HPS appears to mainly moderate age-related WM performance of attentional control and not necessarily of WMC. This suggests different age-related patterns of cognitive functioning across these groups, with higher performance in the HPS- group. Although cross-sectional, our findings further our understanding of cognitive functioning across age and across mental disorders with psychosis.

title: Uncovering Critical Biomarkers, Immune Signatures, and Drug Candidates in Thyroid Cancer: A Systems Biology Approach.
journal: Omics : a journal of integrative biology
abstract: Thyroid cancer (THCA) is the most common endocrine malignancy associated with clinical challenges like recurrence, aggressive variants, and therapy resistance. This study employed an integrative systems-biology approach to interrogate The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA)-THCA transcriptomic data to identify candidate genes and drug-target relationships for THCA. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified and used to construct protein-protein interaction and gene regulatory network (GRN) as well as generate topological, clustering, and enrichment analyses. Candidate genes were interrogated using survival analysis, genetic alteration, correlation, immune infiltration, drug-gene interaction, and molecular docking. Findings were independently validated in two Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) cohorts. A total of 424 DEGs (191 up-regulated, 233 down-regulated) were identified. Seven candidate genes, DPP4, GABRB2, HMGA2, SERPINA1, ADH1B, KLHDC8A, and DLG2, were prioritized, and enrichment analyses revealed functional associations with extracellular matrix remodeling, MAPK signaling, cell-junction regulation, and synaptic signaling. These candidate genes displayed immune infiltration disparities and differential expression in independent GEO datasets. Docking simulations predicted favorable binding geometries for Sitagliptin-DPP4 and Flumazenil-GABRB2, while 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations further authenticated the binding affinities of these two complexes. In conclusion, we identified independent candidate genes and in-silico prioritized drug-target interactions for further preclinical investigations of THCA.

title: Decoding and Rewiring Neurovascular Communication in Spinal Cord Injury via Computational Extracellular Vesicle Dynamics.
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts the neurovascular unit (NVU), notably impairing the blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB), which undergoes a biphasic transformation from acute hyperpermeability to chronic fibrotic sclerosis. This dynamic remodeling creates a heterogeneous barrier that hinders effective drug delivery and limits therapeutic success. Here we integrate pathological characterization with computational molecular dynamics to rationally engineer extracellular vesicles (EVs) capable of receptor-mediated transcytosis across the fibrotic BSCB. Coupled with computational fluid dynamics-optimized hydrogel scaffolds and neuromodulation techniques, this approach promotes NVU repair, restores synaptic homeostasis, and facilitates neural circuit rewiring. This integrated framework advances precision SCI interventions by overcoming the evolving BSCB, offering a novel paradigm for enhancing functional recovery after traumatic SCI and informing therapeutic strategies for central nervous system disorders characterized by barrier dysfunction.

title: Golgi-Linked Glucosylceramide Metabolism Regulates Cocaine-Induced Dendritic Membrane Remodeling.
abstract: Structural plasticity remodeling in the nucleus accumbens plays a critical role in the persistent addictive neurobehaviors induced by cocaine; however, the mechanisms underlying the supply of plasma membrane materials required for these adaptive changes have remained elusive. Here we identified a Golgi-centered lipid metabolic program that enables cocaine-induced structural plasticity in the nucleus accumbens. Cocaine increased glucosylceramide synthase (GCS) expression and glucosylceramide (GlcCer) abundance in dopamine D1 receptor-expressing medium spiny neurons (D1-MSNs) selectively, accompanied by Golgi remodeling and an increased abundance of Golgi-associated vesicles. GlcCer also accumulated in membrane-associated compartments, redistributed toward MAP2-positive dendritic structures, and altered the postsynaptic density architecture. Pharmacological GCS inhibition attenuated cocaine-induced Golgi remodeling and membrane-associated GlcCer accumulation, whereas Ugcg knockdown or D1-MSNs-specific deletion reduced cocaine-induced dendritic and behavioral adaptations. Conversely, exogenous GlcCer treatment restored dendritic remodeling and neurobehavioral responses following Ugcg knockdown. These findings define a D1-MSN-selective Golgi-lipid remodeling program that links GCS-GlcCer metabolism and membrane lipid redistribution to cocaine-induced neuroplasticity.

title: [Evaluation of the efficacy and tolerance of home-based non-invasive ventilation: A review of the literature and expert opinion: The 2023 guidelines of the Groupe Assistance Ventilatoire et Oxygénothérapie (GAVO2) of the Société de Pneumologie de Langue Française (SPLF)].
abstract: Applying the Choosing Wisely® methodology, a task force mandated by the Ventilation and Oxygen-therapy group (GAVO2) of the French Pulmonary Society (SPLF) was commissioned to draw up a series of expert recommendations on practical aspects of long-term non-invasive ventilation (NIV). These guidelines are annually updated. Several themes were taken up, notably including NIV configuration, efficacy and tolerance. For each topic, the experts reviewed recent data in the literature. Based on these data and on their own clinical experience, the experts developed a comprehensive analysis of recent insights, and went on to write out practical tips, which have been grouped together in a series of three articles, of which the first is dedicated to the monitoring of non-invasive ventilation.

title: Beyond B-DNA: the biology of Z-DNA and Z-RNA recognition.
abstract: Z-DNA and Z-RNA (Z-NAs) have long been regarded as rare alternative structures of uncertain in vivo relevance. However, accumulating evidence demonstrates their formation across diverse biological systems. Only a limited number of proteins have been validated as direct, conformation-selective Z-NA binders. Proteins may also stabilize Z-states or promote transitions into or out of them, respond to the surrounding topological conditions, or associate indirectly with Z-prone loci. In this article, we propose five potentially overlapping modes of engagement for Z-NA-associated proteins: conformation readers, stabilizers, conformational remodelers, topology-coupled factors, and context-dependent interactors. By linking canonical Zα readers with topoisomerases, chromatin factors, immune sensors, and viral antagonists, this framework provides a basis for mechanistic classification, experimental validation, and future discovery.

title: The role of transposable elements in primate neurodevelopment and human brain evolution.
abstract: The genetic basis of human brain evolution remains unclear. Transposable elements (TEs), which comprise half the human genome, are emerging as an important source of regulatory innovation. Comparative genomics, single-cell multi-omics, and primate stem cell models show that evolutionarily young primate-specific TEs serve as regulatory elements during brain development. Here we review evidence that TE-derived sequences and Krüppel-associated box zinc finger protein-TE interactions shape neurodevelopment, supporting a model in which evolving TE landscapes and host repressors build lineage- and species-specific regulatory networks in the primate brain. We also discuss technical barriers to causal inference, including repeat-aware mapping, locus-specific perturbation, and incomplete primate genomic resources. Together, these advances provide a framework for determining whether and how TEs contribute to primate neurodevelopment and the roles these elements played in human brain evolution.

title: Sudden Traumatic Noise Exposure Induces an Altered Wave I in the Auditory Brainstem Response in Human.
abstract: Noise trauma may induce auditory symptoms and temporary or permanent shifts in hearing thresholds, assessed with a tone audiogram. Until recently it has been assumed that primary changes after noise trauma exclusively represent damage to the sensory hair cells. Contrary, animal studies have now shown early alterations in auditory brainstem response (ABR) characteristic of auditory neuropathy (AN), as reduction or absence of wave I, following noise trauma. AN involves a variety of disease mechanisms in the cochlea and auditory nerve, affecting the synaptic encoding and/or neural transmission of auditory information. The aim of this study was to evaluate whether patients exposed to noise trauma exhibit click ABR alterations characteristic of AN. Thirty-one adult patients who attended an ear-nose and throat clinic, after a noise trauma, were included and an age- and gender-matched control group of 31 adults was constructed. To evaluate audiologic hearing impairment pure tone audiometry, speech intelligibility, click ABR and transient evoked otoacoustic emissions (TEOAE)/cochlear microphonics (CM) were performed. A full linear mixed model including the interaction between sex and group was tested. Our study showed that individuals exposed to sudden and distinct traumatic noise exhibit a statistically significant reduction (81.1 nV, p < 0.001) in the amplitude of wave I in ABR. We suggest that the hearing investigation after sudden traumatic noise exposure should therefore be expanded with ABR to confirm or exclude AN.

title: Reading Abilities and Visual Evoked Potentials in Hearing-Impaired Children: A Comparative Study of Cochlear Implant and Hearing Aid Users.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate reading comprehension skills, visual evoked potentials (VEP), and saccadic eye movements in hearing aid (HA) users, cochlear implant (CI) users, and individuals with normal hearing (NH), to investigate the relationship between sensory processing and reading ability. The study included 45 participants, 15 HA users, 15 CI users, and 15 NH. VEP, a saccadic test, and a reading comprehension test were performed. VEP recordings were conducted with and without the hearing device for HA and CI users. Reading comprehension scores in the CI group were significantly lower than those in the NH and HA groups (p < 0.001). Rightward saccade velocity was consistently lower than leftward velocity across all groups. Notably, VEP amplitudes in HA users (N1-P1: p = 0.048) and CI users (N1-P1: p = 0.005, 0.019, 0.001; P1-N2: p = 0.010, 0.008, 0.022) were significantly larger in the unaided condition (without device) compared to the aided condition. Correlation analyses did not reveal a consistent pattern of association between reading comprehension scores and VEP parameters. While reading skills were found to be weaker in the CI group, the absence of a direct correlation between VEP/saccadic parameters and reading scores suggests that lower level sensory processing and higher order reading comprehension may operate through distinct mechanisms. The increased VEP amplitudes observed without hearing devices suggest a cross-modal neuroplastic compensation in the visual cortex during auditory deprivation.

title: Immediate transcranial magnetic stimulation-evoked potentials reveal short-latency intracortical inhibition.
abstract: Short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) is the most widely used neurophysiological index of GABAergic inhibition in the human cortex. However, it is an indirect measure, inferring synaptic inhibition from suppression of peripherally recorded motor-evoked potentials (MEPs) elicited by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). In the standard protocol, a subthreshold conditioning pulse suppresses the MEP evoked by a suprathreshold test pulse delivered 1-5 ms later. Interpretation is further complicated by temporal overlap with short-interval intracortical facilitation (SICF), reflecting excitatory interactions at interstimulus intervals of ∼1.5 and 2.7 ms. To overcome these limitations, we recorded immediate TMS-evoked EEG potentials (iTEPs; 1-10 ms post-stimulus) as a more direct measure of motor cortical activity in 16 healthy volunteers (20-35 years; seven male). The conventional SICI protocol suppressed only later components of the iTEP, probably corresponding to late corticospinal volleys previously identified in epidural spinal recordings after suprathreshold TMS, while the earliest iTEP component was unaffected. Importantly, later iTEPs were suppressed to a similar extent whether conditioning-test intervals coincided with SICF peaks or troughs, and the magnitude of iTEP suppression correlated with concurrently recorded paired-pulse MEP suppression. SICI also reduced an early TEP component (N15; 10-20 ms), but paired-pulse N15 suppression showed a different dependence on stimulus intensity and did not correlate with MEP suppression. These findings demonstrate that SICI measured via MEPs does not reflect a global index of cortical GABAergic motor cortical inhibition but instead reflects inhibition within specific cortical circuits that can be investigated more directly with iTEPs. KEY POINTS: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the primary motor cortex evokes high-frequency activity in the corticospinal tract, which can be measured directly with invasive, epidural recordings or indirectly as a time-locked, compound EMG response [i.e. motor evoked potential (MEP)]. GABAergic intracortical inhibition can be indexed as the MEP suppression caused by a subthreshold TMS pulse preceding the suprathreshold pulse by 1-5 ms. Combining TMS with artifact-minimized EEG allows the assessment of paired-pulse inhibition of immediate and early peaks of TMS-evoked EEG potential (TEP). Both immediate TEP (iTEP) and early TEP peaks display paired-pulse inhibition but only iTEP suppression relates to MEP suppression. iTEPs enable investigations of intracortical interactions non-invasively at the cortical level, which enables assessment of cortical and corticospinal physiology with TMS even in the absence of MEPs.

title: Spontaneous Intermolecular Cross-Linking Produces Aβ Dimers With Multiple Alzheimer's Disease Relevant Activities.
abstract: Despite success of therapies targeting the amyloid β-protein (Aβ), the molecular identity of the forms of Aβ which contribute to Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains poorly understood. SDS-stable Aβ dimers are present in higher-order aggregates and exert disease-relevant toxicity, but whether dimers form before or after large aggregates, or how dimers contribute to AD pathogenesis were previously unknown. Here, we report that covalently cross-linked Aβ1-42 dimers can form spontaneously upon prolonged incubation of Aβ fibrils and contain isopeptide bonds (Asp1-Glu22 and Asp1-Asp1), the same as those identified in dimers found in AD brain. Importantly, dimer-enriched Aβ aggregates (DEBA) are structurally distinct to dimer-poor aggregates (DPBA) and have enhanced resistance to proteolysis. Functionally, DEBA exhibit stronger binding to microglia, induce transcription of key pro-inflammatory cytokines, nucleate into plaque-like structures with microglia in vitro, and exacerbate amyloid deposition in AppNL-F/NL-F mice. DEBA do not appear to be overtly neurotoxic, whereas solubilized DEBA induce toxicities reminiscent of that caused by Aβ-containing AD brain extract. These findings demonstrate prolonged incubation of fibrillar Aβ aggregates results in spontaneous formation of cross-linked dimers, and this is associated with changes in aggregate morphology and emergence of multiple disease-relevant activities.

title: Explanatory models of mental illness among tribal communities in the Attappady region of Kerala: An exploratory qualitative study.
journal: Australasian psychiatry : bulletin of Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists
abstract: ObjectiveTo explore explanatory models of mental illness among the Irula, Muduga, and Kurumba communities in the Attappady region of Kerala and to understand how these beliefs influence perceptions of illness and help-seeking.MethodsA qualitative descriptive study was conducted among 26 adults from the Irula, Muduga, and Kurumba communities in the Attappady region of Kerala. Participants included community members, family caregivers, traditional healers, and community leaders. Semi-structured interviews were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis.ResultsFour themes emerged. Participants explained mental health problems through (1) supernatural explanations, including divine punishment, spirit possession, and black magic; (2) environmental explanations such as seasonal changes and heat; (3) psychosocial explanations, such as grief, financial hardship, and family conflict; and (4) pluralistic help-seeking, combining traditional healing and biomedical services.ConclusionsAmong participants from the Irula, Muduga and Kurumba communities in the Attappady region of Kerala, mental illness was understood through interconnected supernatural, environmental and psychosocial explanations. Help-seeking involved traditional healing and biomedical services, with families and elders influencing decisions. Culturally specific explanatory models should be explored during psychiatric assessment and treatment planning. Findings may not apply to other tribal or Indigenous populations.

title: Detecting Interventional Spatiotemporal Causality in Dynamical Systems.
abstract: Causal interactions in dynamical systems are structured not only across variables but also across time. However, conventional causal representations typically collapse this temporal organization into variable-level links, obscuring when causal influences act. Here we introduce interventional spatiotemporal causality (ISTC), a framework that represents causal organization over the joint space of variables and temporal delays. ISTC reconstructs the high-dimensional state space of a dynamical system from observations, learns a digital twin of the embedded dynamics, and performs targeted interventions within the learned dynamics to quantify intervention responses. Synthetic benchmarks show accurate recovery of causal topology and characteristic delays, while real-world applications reveal interpretable spatiotemporal patterns of inferred causal influence consistent with domain knowledge. The framework integrates three key features: Joint modeling of causal relationships across spatial and temporal dimensions, intervention-based inference grounded in reconstructed dynamical mechanisms, and a flexible state-space reconstruction strategy that balances causal resolution with computational efficiency. By making the temporal organization of causal interactions directly accessible, ISTC provides a general framework for characterizing causal dependencies in complex spatiotemporal dynamical systems.

title: Physical activity coaching and text messaging for adults with mobility limitations (ComeBACK): hybrid type 1 effectiveness implementation randomised controlled trial.
abstract: To evaluate the effectiveness of a physical activity coaching intervention compared with text messaging intervention and waitlist control in adults with mobility limitations. Three arm, pragmatic, superiority, hybrid type 1 effectiveness implementation randomised controlled trial. Health services and general communities across five Australian states, 19 December 2018 to 7 March 2023. 512 community dwelling adults (≥18 years) who self-reported mobility limitations (difficulty or inability to walk 800 m, with or without a walking aid) but were still able to leave home without physical assistance from another person. Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1 allocation ratio to: a six month, multicomponent intervention including fortnightly physiotherapist delivered telephone coaching (coaching group, n=172); a six month, multicomponent intervention including regular unidirectional text messages (texting group, n=171); and no intervention for six months, followed by the six month text messaging intervention (waitlist control group, n=169). Participants and physiotherapists were unmasked to group allocation. The primary outcome was device measured mean daily steps at six months, analysed according to treatment allocation using all available data. Outcome assessors and data analysts were masked to group allocation. Participants' mean age was 69 years (standard deviation (SD) 10 years) and 76% (n=388/511) were women. More than half (n=263/508, 51%) of participants reported multiple long term conditions as the main reason for their mobility limitation. At six months, mean daily steps were 931 higher (95% confidence interval 409 to 1452 steps; P=0.001) in the coaching group (mean 7256 (SD 3736) steps) compared with waitlist group (6526 (3003) steps); and 571 steps higher (58 to 1084, P=0.03) compared with the texting group (6529 (3029) steps). Mean daily steps in the texting group were 359 higher (-91 to 810, P=0.12) compared with the waitlist group, but this was not statistically significant. The number of adverse events was similar between groups (11/172 (6%) in the coaching group, 7/171 (4%) in the texting group, and 13/169 (8%) in the waitlist group) and none were serious. A person centred coaching intervention produced modest increases in physical activity and was more effective than a less intensive texting intervention or no intervention among adults with mobility limitations. Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12618001983291.

title: Long-Term Neuromodulatory Effects on the Ionic Current Parameter Space of Oscillatory Neurons.
abstract: Neurons are constantly subject to short-term neuromodulatory effects through the regulation of various proteins, including ion channels. However, the long-term influences of neuromodulators on ion channels remain poorly understood. Multiple ionic currents work in concert to generate oscillatory neuronal activity, and long-term neuromodulatory effects on them likely differ from short-term effects. Here we examined the long-term effects of the neuromodulatory environment on the ionic conductances that generate the rhythmic activity of the pyloric network of male crabs, Cancer borealis We measured most of the known voltage-dependent and synaptic currents expressed by two identified pyloric neurons in their normal neuromodulatory environment and after prolonged removal of neuromodulators. To understand the global conductance makeup of these cells, we defined the conductance parameter space of each cell as the multidimensional volume occupied by its conductances in a population of identical neurons. We then examined the changes in this volume after independently modifying both the neuromodulator environment and activity of these neurons. Our results reveal that neuromodulation, and, to some extent, activity appear to constrain the conductance parameter space in pyloric neurons, suggesting a general phenomenon. Interestingly, while neuromodulators appear to exert a similar regulatory effect on both cells, activity seems to do so in a cell-type-specific manner. Our results suggest a mechanism that explains why the same manipulation of the neuromodulatory input does not produce the same change in network activity across animals: the degeneracy of the pacemaker mechanism.Significance Statement How does a rhythm-generating neuronal network recover its rhythm after its disruption? Neuromodulators control neuronal activity, especially rhythmic activity, which is vital to animals. Thus, network robustness and the ability to recover from major perturbations are of crucial importance. We tested the hypothesis that neuromodulators constrain the entire neuronal ionic conductance parameter space in a well-characterized rhythm-generating network. Our results confirm that neuromodulators and activity regulate the global neuronal conductance landscape. Our results suggest a mechanism that explains why the same manipulation of the neuromodulatory environment produces distinct effects on network activity across individuals: the degeneracy of the pacemaker mechanism. These results support the need to consider individualized approaches to understand functional mechanisms and to develop therapies for pathological conditions.

title: Gabapentinoid Exposure and Persistent Postoperative Opioid Use After Lumbar Spinal Fusion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
authors: da Silva Moura Costa Antônio Olímpio
abstract: Gabapentinoids are used in multimodal analgesia, but their association with persistent opioid use after lumbar fusion remains uncertain. This systematic review and meta-analysis compared adults exposed to gabapentin or pregabalin with unexposed patients. The primary outcome was persistent opioid use or prescription. Inpatient opioid consumption, postoperative pain, and disability were assessed as secondary outcomes. The PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library databases were searched through 30 August 2026. Comparative studies of adults undergoing spinal fusion were eligible if they evaluated gabapentinoid exposure vs no exposure under usual care or a comparable opioid-based regimen. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using ROBINS-I. Cohorts with a high probability of overlap were not included together in the same pooled estimates. Random-effects models estimated risk ratios (RRs) and mean differences (MDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Six retrospective cohort studies involving patients undergoing lumbar fusion were included. Gabapentinoid exposure was not significantly associated with persistent opioid use or prescription at the longest compatible follow-up (RR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.89-1.19; P = 0.67) or at 3-6 months (RR, 1.03; 95% CI, 0.81-1.32; P = 0.73). There were also no significant differences in inpatient opioid consumption (MD, 43.13 morphine milligram equivalents; 95% CI, -9.72 to 95.99; P = 0.07) or change in the Oswestry Disability Index at 12 months (MD, 2.73 points; 95% CI, -8.54 to 14.00; P = 0.41). Findings for persistent opioid use were consistent in temporal and publication-level sensitivity analyses. Observational evidence showed no statistically significant association between gabapentinoid exposure and persistent opioid use or prescription after lumbar fusion. There were also no significant differences in inpatient opioid consumption or 12-month changes in back pain, leg pain, or disability scores. Gabapentinoid use should remain individualized; these findings do not establish a benefit in reducing long-term opioid use after lumbar fusion. PROSPERO CRD420261493895.

title: Why and When to Adjust for Intracranial Volume in Structural Brain Imaging.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
abstract: Structural neuroimaging research is marked by substantial methodological variability, with important implications for inference and reproducibility. A central but often under-justified source for this variability is whether intracranial volume (ICV) is included as a covariate. We argue that ICV adjustment is not a neutral analytical step, but a modeling decision that fundamentally alters the research question by redefining the variance under investigation, and it can even change the very direction of the estimated effect. We evaluate five common research questions in the literature and argue that each is underpinned by distinct assumptions about where ICV sits in the causal structure linking neuroanatomy with other complex behavioral traits. We identify contexts in which ICV adjustment is necessary to define the construct under study, as well as situations in which it removes meaningful variance or introduces interpretational and statistical complications. We argue that ICV adjustment should explicitly be justified, and we provide practical guidance for deciding when such adjustment is appropriate. We hope to stimulate debate and improve consistency, interpretability, and reproducibility of population-level neuroimaging research.

title: Computational Insights into Afferent Integration Underlying Mechanical Allodynia.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience

title: Salient Objects in a Scene Benefit From Enhanced Memory Encoding: Neural Evidence for a Spatial von Restorff Effect.
abstract: Rapidly detecting salient objects from our surroundings and learning their behavioral relevance is crucial for human survival. The present study tested the hypothesis that rapid learning of these salient objects in visual search arrays is possible because they trigger von Restorff-like effects. We required participants to detect tilted target bars among distractors while we recorded their electroencephalograms (EEGs). We first replicated previous findings by showing that the most salient targets elicited the strongest multivariate decoding, as well as univariate indices of attentional selection (i.e., the N2pc component). Importantly for our learning hypothesis, early selection of highly salient targets (25° tilt) triggered a cascade of preferential processing downstream, marked by stronger CDA and P3b components, neural synchronization, and phase-amplitude coupling between low- and high-frequency activity, along with better recall performance of target orientation. Trial-by-trial coupling strength predicted subsequent N2pc amplitude, linking memory-related activity to future attentional deployment. Overall, the present study demonstrates that object salience in spatial arrays drives a cascade of processing, facilitating rapid learning of object relevance while humans search their environment, similar to the classic demonstrations of the von Restorff effect, except the objects are distributed in space rather than time.

title: Direct Electro-Optic Transduction of Neurophysiological Signals for Multichannel Recording Using Ion-Gated Graphene Integrated Photonics.
abstract: Large-scale neural recording with high spatiotemporal resolution is essential for mapping distributed brain activity. However, scaling the number of simultaneously recorded channels in implantable electrical probes places growing demand on interconnects, multiplexing, and readout electronics. Functional optical imaging enables parallel readout but requires fluorescent labels or genetic modification. Emerging label-free optical approaches rely on bulky free-space configurations or surface-level detection. Here, we introduce an ion-gated graphene-integrated photonic platform that directly transduces neurophysiological signals into wavelength-multiplexed optical channels. The sensor integrates monolayer graphene with an on-chip photonic microresonator. Extracellular potentials modulate graphene's electrochemical potential through the graphene-electrolyte electrical double layer. This change in graphene's electrochemical potential modulates its absorption and thereby alters the optical transmission through the resonator-coupled waveguide. This mechanism enables optical encoding of neural signals without exogenous labels, genetic modification, or conventional electrode-based electrical readout. Because each microresonator can operate at a distinct wavelength, arrays of sensors can share a single bus waveguide using wavelength-division multiplexing. We demonstrate a detection limit of 20 µV at a signal-to-noise ratio of 3 dB and show label-free recording of evoked neurophysiological signals from mouse brain tissue, including multiplexed recording from 10 sensors along a single waveguide. These results establish ion-gated graphene-integrated photonics as a compact and scalable platform for wavelength-multiplexed, label-free neural recording and future implantable photonic neural interfaces.

title: Extended window thrombolysis (4.5-24 hours) in acute ischaemic stroke: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
journal: Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry

title: Parietal GABA in individuals with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and asymptomatic C9orf72 repeat expansion carriers assessed with MR spectroscopy at 7 T.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease. Multiple pathways are involved in its pathophysiology, but the exact mechanisms are still unknown. In this study, we investigate the role of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) in ALS and the related C9orf72 repeat expansion (C9). As the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter, GABA may affect hyperexcitability in ALS. Decreased GABA levels have been reported in the motor cortex in ALS, but neither regions outside the motor area nor carriers of ALS-related pathogenic genetic variants were investigated. We used GABA-edited magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MEGA-sLASER) at 7 T to examine ratios of GABA to creatine. We compared individuals with ALS (n = 17) to controls (n = 13) and separately compare asymptomatic C9orf72 repeat expansion carriers (n = 5) to non-carriers (n = 7) from a single family. We placed the voxel of interest in the parietal lobe as it is specifically at risk in C9 carriers. We found no statistically significant differences in mean GABA ratios in either comparison, but individuals with ALS showed a higher variance than controls (p = 0.026). We conclude that parietal GABA is not involved in ALS pathology in all individuals with ALS, but increased variance indicates heterogeneity and may reflect subgroups with GABAergic dysfunction.

title: Multidimensional profiling of bitterness responsiveness reveals distinct response profiles beyond PROP status.
abstract: Bitterness responsiveness varies substantially among individuals and may not be adequately represented by conventional 6-n-propylthiouracil (PROP) taster status. This study characterized multidimensional responses to multiple bitter stimuli and examined their oral physiological, dietary, and genetic correlates. A total of 262 Korean women aged 20-39 years rated the bitterness of quercetin, food-grade aloe vera powder, caffeine, quinine hydrochloride, and PROP using the general Labeled Magnitude Scale once per stimulus in each of three weekly sessions. Z-score-standardized mean ratings were analyzed using agglomerative hierarchical clustering. Internal validation and resampling stability supported two groups with higher or lower overall bitterness ratings. Five exploratory subgroups described stimulus-specific patterns within these groups. One subgroup had relatively low PROP ratings but elevated ratings for several other stimuli; another had the lowest mean ratings for most other stimuli but not for PROP. Fungiform and circumvallate papillae counts, and total salivary protein concentration did not differ significantly between the two groups or between the latter subgroup and the remaining participants after false discovery rate correction. No dietary differences remained significant in overall comparisons between the two groups or five subgroups; however, in an exploratory comparison, the latter subgroup reported more frequent coffee consumption than the remaining participants (adjusted p = 0.0057). In the genotyped subset (n = 174; n = 172 for common-diplotype comparisons), TAS2R38 diplotype associations remained significant only for PROP after correction. In the full sensory cohort, PROP status alone did not capture the full range of bitterness-response patterns. The five subgroups remain exploratory and require independent replication.

title: Antipsychotic Use in Bipolar Disorder.
journal: Child and adolescent psychiatric clinics of North America
abstract: Pediatric (bipolar disorder) BD carries substantial morbidity, including prolonged symptom burden, high rates of suicide attempts and substance use, and psychosocial impairment. Accurate diagnosis requires careful longitudinal assessment, as presentations in youth often differ from adults, with more rapid cycling, mixed features, and irritability over classic euphoric mania. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to reduce potential impairment and to support early recovery of youth with BD. The purpose of this article is to discuss the use of antipsychotics in the treatment of pediatric BD.

title: Clozapine in Children and Adolescents: Indications, Efficacy, and Safety.
journal: Child and adolescent psychiatric clinics of North America
abstract: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic but it remains underutilized. This review synthesizes evidence for clozapine use in children and adolescents, including additional indications such as suicidality, aggression, autism, and catatonia. Children have differences in pharmacokinetics, dosing, and side effect profiles. Although side effects can include agranulocytosis, myocarditis, and metabolic effects, regular laboratory and vital sign monitoring and adjunctive treatments can mitigate these risks. Persistent barriers often delay initiation, but increased education and systems-level changes can reduce barriers to clozapine use. Recent regulatory changes and emerging evidence support earlier and more widespread use of clozapine in appropriately selected pediatric populations.

title: [Forensic chemical analysis of carbaryl].
abstract: To develop a technique for the determination of carbaryl and its main metabolite 1-naphthol in the tissues of biological organs and blood, applicable in the practice of forensic chemical analysis. Experimental studies were carried out using extraction, TLC, refined chromatography of ordinary pressure, HPLC and GC-MS. The isolation of carbaryl and 1-naphthol from biological matrices was carried out by insisting with a mixture of ethyl acetate-acetone (5:5) in conditions when the amount of insulating fluid exceeded the amount of the studied matrix by half by weight. The appropriateness of the analytus from the column (190×10 mm) of silica gel is shown 60ǻ 40/63 μm with a mobile phase of hexane-acetone (8:2), which has formed the basis of the developed option for cleaning the carbaryl and 1-naphthol extracted from bio-meters. The advantages of the system of carbon tetrachloride-diethyl ether (5:5) as a mobile phase during the identification of these compounds by the nature of their mobility in the thin layer of silica gel (sorbfil plates) are experimentally proven. To determine the carbaryl and 1-naphthol using HPLC, an analytical column (150×3.9 mm) Nova Pack C-18 and eluent - water-methanol-acetonitrile (70:5:25 by volume). As the main method of confirming the analytical identification, GC-MS was used (helium as a mobile phase, a stationary phase based on dimethylpolysiloxane with phenyl substituents (5%) in the column with dimensions of 30 m×0.25 mm). The carbaryl mass spectrum included the signals of the following charged particles (m/z): 40, 51, 58, 63, 72, 89, 98, 115, 144, 156, 178, 190, mass spectrum of the 1-naphthol-particle signals (m/z): 40, 51, 58, 63, 72, 98, 115, 126, 144 performed series. Evaluation experiments allowed to confirm the compliance of the developed techniques with key validation parameters. The limits of the detection of carbaryl of 100 g of the organ (liver) and blood - 0.014 and 0.012 mg, the limits of quantitative determination - 0.028 and 0.022 mg. The limits of the detection of 1-naphthol for the liver and blood are equal to 0.018 and 0.014 mg, respectively, the limits of the quantitative determination-0.034 and 0.026 mg. The study of the bio-meters of the corpse of a person who died of carbaryl poisoning has shown that the most carbaryl and its metabolite are present in the stomach with contents, kidneys, duodenum with contents and liver with the General extent, to a lesser extent - in the blood and brain.

title: Characteristic basal ganglia injury in fentanyl- and cocaine-related hypoxic brain injury: a case report.
abstract: We present the case of a 33-year-old woman who developed bilateral basal ganglia injury following a hypoxic brain injury in the setting of fentanyl and cocaine use. Notably, she never required intubation and received only minimal supplemental oxygen, yet MRI demonstrated bilateral basal ganglia diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) with corresponding T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, findings most associated with significant ischemic injury. Rather than the movement disorders typically seen with basal ganglia lesions, her predominant presentation was neuropsychiatric, characterized by apathy, impulsivity, and risk-taking behavior. Drawing on the mechanistic overlap with traumatic brain injury affecting Prefrontal cortical (PFC) and subcortical networks, she was treated with a novel combination of guanfacine, bupropion, and N-acetylcysteine (NAC), targeting executive dysfunction, apathy, and neuroinflammatory pathways, respectively. This case highlights a rare neuropsychiatric presentation of drug-related hypoxic basal ganglia injury and provides a framework for understanding and treating the behavioral sequelae of such injury. It also adds to a small but growing body of literature linking opioid overdose to characteristic basal ganglia diffusion restriction, even in the absence of overt hypoxia.

title: Treatment outcomes and safety of oral β-blockers and sirolimus in children with kaposiform hemangioendothelioma: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
abstract: To describe outcomes and safety of oral β-blockers and sirolimus in children with kaposiform hemangioendothelioma (KHE). We retrospectively reviewed children with KHE receiving oral β-blockers or sirolimus at Beijing Children's Hospital from January 2016 to April 2026. Lesion regression at fixed time points, treatment duration, treatment discontinuation, recurrence, and safety were assessed. Thirteen patients received β-blockers and 11 sirolimus, including three with prior therapy. Baseline lesion measurements did not differ significantly, but the β-blocker group was younger [median 4.0 (IQR, 3.0-4.0) vs. 19.0 (10.5-29.5) months; p 25%, >50%, and >75% regression occurred in 76.9%, 46.2%, and 23.1% with β-blockers versus 100.0%, 72.7%, and 18.2% with sirolimus, respectively. Treatment was discontinued in 9/13 and 3/11 patients (median durations, 40.0 and 18.0 months, respectively). No recurrence was observed after cessation. Safety events were reversible and manageable. In this cohort, both treatments were associated with improvement, but baseline imbalances limit direct comparison. β-blocker responses in predominantly younger, less symptomatic patients require confirmation in larger prospective studies.

title: Early-Life Movement Behaviour Patterns and Later Clinically Diagnosed Obesity: A Longitudinal Analysis.
abstract: To investigate the longitudinal association between early-life movement behaviour patterns and later clinically diagnosed obesity. In the population-based All Babies in Southeast Sweden (ABIS) cohort, 16 415 children were included after consent. A total of 542 participants had an obesity diagnosis recorded in the Swedish National Patient Register through 2023. Questionnaire-based movement behaviour data were collected at ages 3, 5, 8, 10-12 and 17-23 years. A Total Activity Score (TAS) combining physical activity and sedentary behaviours was used to classify participants as less active or highly active. Cox proportional hazards regression estimated hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals, adjusting for maternal education and parental body mass index. Higher TAS was associated with a lower hazard of clinically diagnosed obesity from age 5 onwards. Adjusted HRs for highly active versus less active participants were 0.85 (0.62-0.97, p = 0.003) at age 5, 0.66 (0.43-0.78, p = 0.002) at age 8, 0.54 (0.38-0.67, p = 0.001) at age 10-12 and 0.49 (0.23-0.59, p = 0.001) at age 17-23. Associations were observed in both sexes, without formal interaction testing. Favourable childhood movement behaviour patterns were associated with a lower hazard of clinically diagnosed obesity.

title: Dexmedetomidine Dosing Evaluation for Sedation in Neonates Undergoing Therapeutic Hypothermia.
abstract: Recently, dexmedetomidine has replaced opioids for sedation in neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) patients with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE). The study objectives were to describe dosing patterns, evaluate compliance, and compare effectiveness and safety between the original (pre-implementation) and revised (post-implementation) in-house dexmedetomidine dosing guidelines.
