title: Brain-Computer Interface: Exploring Alternative Solutions for Neurological Disorders.
abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) refers to a system that enables direct communication between the brain and external devices. Although the concept of BCI was introduced over 50 years ago, recent advancements in hardware technology and decoding algorithms have accelerated its development significantly. In the realm of neurological disorders, BCI has shown great potential as a tool for diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation, and functional compensation. This chapter provides a comprehensive review of BCI applications in neurological disorders, covering aspects such as diagnosis and prognosis, therapeutic interventions, rehabilitation strategies, and restoration of impaired functions. These developments highlight the practicality and effectiveness of BCI in offering adaptable solutions for patients with neurological conditions. Nonetheless, further research is essential to address ongoing technical, clinical, and ethical challenges to fully realize the potential of BCI technology.

title: Astrocytic Gq Signaling in Mice Enhances Glial Engagement With Amyloid Plaques and Promotes Plaque Clearance In Vivo.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by the progressive accumulation of extracellular amyloid-β (Aβ) plaques, aberrant tau phosphorylation and aggregation, neuroinflammation, and cognitive decline, with growing evidence implicating glial dysfunction as a key driver of disease progression. While astrocytes and microglia accumulate around Aβ plaques and influence their clearance, the intracellular signaling pathways that regulate these glial responses in vivo remain poorly defined. We investigated whether sustained activation of Gq-coupled signaling in astrocytes or microglia modulates amyloid pathology in humanized amyloid precursor protein (App) knock-in mouse models of AD. Amyloid mouse models were crossed with tamoxifen-inducible transgenic lines expressing the hM3Dq designer receptor in either astrocytes or microglia to enable cell-type-specific activation of Gq signaling, to avoid the confound of viral expression in glial cells. Sustained astrocytic Gq signaling significantly increased astrocyte accumulation around plaques and reduced plaque burden in both the cortex and hippocampus. Astrocytic Gq signaling was further associated with Aβ reactivity within both astrocytic and microglial compartments, along with enhanced microglial recruitment and elevated expression of lysosomal/phagocytic markers. In contrast, chronic activation of microglial Gq signaling alone did not measurably alter Aβ plaque burden under the experimental conditions tested. Together, these findings demonstrate that astrocytic Gq signaling is sufficient to reprogram plaque-associated glial interactions toward a clearance-associated phenotype in vivo. Our results identify astrocytic Gq signaling as an important regulator of the multicellular plaque environment and a potential pathway for modulating glial responses in Alzheimer's disease.

title: Is Schneiderian phenomenology an interface between bipolar disorder and schizophrenia? Neurocognitive and neuroimaging evidence from a cross-sectional comparative study.
abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) and schizophrenia (SZ) show clinical and neurobiological overlap, but the position of psychotic BD within this spectrum remains uncertain. We tested whether BD with Schneiderian first-rank symptoms (P-BD) more closely resembled SZ than BD without lifetime psychosis (NP-BD). Ninety clinically stable participants (30 P-BD, 30 NP-BD and 30 SZ) completed a neurocognitive battery and T1-weighted structural MRI analyzed with vol2Brain. Group differences were tested using omnibus comparisons with corrected post hoc tests. Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction was applied within cognitive and anatomical families. Secondary covariate-adjusted multinomial models were exploratory. SZ showed slower Trail Making Test performance and poorer Auditory Verbal Learning Test total learning and immediate post-interference recall. The verbal-memory findings survived FDR correction; Trail Making Test findings were at the correction threshold. SZ also showed smaller cerebellar vermis measures and reduced occipital-pole thickness relative to P-BD, all of which survived FDR correction. Occipital-pole volume, anterior-insula and opercular findings did not survive correction and were considered exploratory. Secondary multinomial models identified cognitive and regional structural variables associated with diagnostic group, but no validated classifier was developed. The FRS-defined P-BD group did not converge with SZ across cognitive or structural measures. The findings are compatible with partial overlap between BD and SZ alongside quantitative differences, but the small sample, multiple comparisons and absence of a healthy comparison group require cautious interpretation and independent replication.

title: Sex-based differences in glycaemic variability and clinical outcomes among older inpatients with type 2 diabetes: insights from the GLIMPACT study.
abstract: Glycaemic variability (GV) has emerged as a potential marker of adverse outcomes in hospitalised patients with diabetes, yet its clinical impact in older adults and the role of sex differences remain unclear. To evaluate the association between in-hospital GV and length of stay (LOS) and one- and two-year all-cause mortality in older adults with type 2 diabetes, and to explore sex-specific patterns. Retrospective observational study of patients aged ≥ 65 years with type 2 diabetes admitted to a geriatric unit (2018-2020). GV was assessed using the coefficient of variation (CV) of point-of-care glucose measurements (POCT). Multivariable linear regression and Cox proportional hazards models were applied, adjusting for relevant confounders, with analyses stratified by sex. A total of 283 patients (59.7% female, mean age 84.9 ± 6.9 years) were included. Higher GV was independently associated with longer LOS in the overall cohort (β = 0.194, 95% CI 0.078-0.310, p = 0.001) and in females, but not in males. Higher GV was associated with increased one-year mortality in females (HR = 1.02, 95% CI 1.00-1.04, p = 0.019), while an inverse association was observed in males. At two years, GV remained associated with mortality only in females. Sex differences in insulin sensitivity and counter-regulatory responses may partly explain these findings. The inverse association in males should be interpreted cautiously, possibly reflecting residual confounding from a higher prevalence of SARS-CoV-2 infection. In-hospital GV was associated with longer hospital stay and higher mortality in older adults with type 2 diabetes, particularly among females, suggesting it may represent a potential marker of clinical vulnerability warranting sex-specific approaches to glycaemic management.

title: Toward an Integrative Process-Based Framework of Psychological Experience.
abstract: Contemporary psychology and cognitive science have generated increasingly sophisticated accounts of cognition, emotion, behavior, embodiment, and neural functioning. At the same time, substantial fragmentation remains across explanatory traditions concerned with lived psychological experience, including constructivist, phenomenological, predictive processing, dynamic systems, affective neuroscience, and clinical process-based perspectives. The present article advances a process-oriented integrative framework intended to synthesize converging insights across these domains while clarifying how psychological experience may be continuously organized in real time across changing states and contexts. The framework proposes two dynamically interrelated generative processes-interpretive activity and experiential rendering-together with intrinsic regulatory potential, a hypothesized potential for reorganization. Interpretive activity refers to the ongoing organization of meaning through which situations, memories, bodily sensations, and anticipations become psychologically significant. Experiential rendering refers to the manner in which interpretations become experientially salient, emotionally compelling, and subjectively real. Intrinsic regulatory potential refers to the conditional capacity for broader, more flexible, and context-responsive reorganization as restrictive organization loosens. Related constructs include experiential authority, experiential constriction, experiential flexibility, state-dependent organization, and affect as directional signaling. Psychological distress is conceptualized not primarily as fixed pathology or static dysfunction, but as varying patterns of experiential organization emerging across changing states and contexts. The article situates the framework in relation to contemporary constructivist, enactive, phenomenological, predictive processing, and dynamic systems perspectives while outlining implications for psychotherapy, resilience, emotional wellbeing, and future process-oriented psychological research.

title: Impaired cellular stress adaptability in Alzheimer's disease patient-derived fibroblasts: a PFKFB3-linked transcriptomic response to oxidative stress.
abstract: Aging-related impairment in cellular stress adaptability may contribute to vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease (AD), but patient-derived experimental models that preserve agingassociated molecular features remain underused. Here, we investigated transcriptomic responses to oxidative stress in ex vivo dermal fibroblasts derived from patients with AD and control participants matched for age and sex. Fibroblasts were exposed to hydrogen peroxide to induce reactive oxygen species-mediated stress, followed by RNA sequencing to identify disease-associated differences in stress-responsive gene regulation. AD-derived fibroblasts exhibited distinct oxidative stress response patterns, with altered regulation of pathways related to endoplasmic reticulum stress, immune activation, autophagy, protein synthesis, and cell cycle control. Systematic candidate gene prioritization identified PFKFB3 as a key stress-responsive gene showing reduced induction in AD fibroblasts. Lower PFKFB3 responsiveness was associated with poorer cognitive performance and higher levels of neurodegeneration-related blood biomarkers, including plasma pTau217, neurofilament light chain, and glial fibrillary acidic protein. In immortalized human astrocytes, PFKFB3 knockdown reduced cell viability under oxidative stress and altered transcriptional programs related to proteostasis, metabolic regulation, and immune activation. These findings suggest that AD is associated with impaired cellular stress adaptability in patient-derived fibroblasts and highlight PFKFB3 as a candidate node linking oxidative stress responsiveness, glial vulnerability, and AD-related pathological burden.

title: Esketamine Mitigates Perioperative Neurocognitive Impairment Through Attenuation of Blood-Brain Barrier Injury By Downregulating C3 Expression in Aged Mice.
abstract: Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PND) are common complications in elderly patients, and blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a key contributing factor. This study investigated the effects of esketamine on postoperative cognitive function, BBB integrity, and complement component C3 (C3) expression in aged mice. Fifteen-month-old male C57BL/6 mice underwent laparotomy under sevoflurane anesthesia to establish a PND model. Animals were randomly assigned to five groups: control (CON), esketamine alone (ES), PND model (PND), PND with esketamine treatment (PND + ES), and PND with esketamine plus exogenous C3 (PND + ES + C3). Cognitive function was assessed using the Morris water maze and Y-maze tests. BBB permeability, ultrastructural alterations, and tight junction protein expression were evaluated in vivo by Evans Blue extravasation, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), Western blotting (WB), and immunofluorescence. In parallel, an in vitro BBB model using bEnd.3 cells was employed to examine the direct effects of esketamine on barrier function through measurements of transendothelial electrical resistance (TEER) and FITC-dextran permeability. Anesthesia and surgery induced significant early postoperative cognitive impairment in aged mice, accompanied by BBB disruption, decreased tight junction protein expression, and elevated C3 levels. Esketamine treatment alleviated cognitive deficits and attenuated BBB injury. Consistently, in vitro studies provided supportive evidence that esketamine enhanced barrier integrity in bEnd.3 cells. These protective effects were accompanied by reduced C3 and C3aR expression. Esketamine attenuated early postoperative cognitive impairment and BBB injury in aged mice, accompanied by reduced C3 expression. These findings suggest a possible contribution of C3-related processes, although the causal involvement of C3a-C3aR signaling remains to be established.

title: Stimulation of plasmin activity by acetylsalicylic acid hinders prion propagation in vitro and in vivo.
journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
abstract: Autocatalytic propagation of PrPSc, the misfolded isoform of the cellular prion protein (PrPC), is the hallmark of fatal, neurodegenerative disorders termed prion diseases. Physiologically, PrPC undergoes α-cleavage, generating C1 and N1 fragments, which disrupts the region necessary for conversion of PrPC to PrPSc. Recently, we reported that plasmin, an enzyme that cleaves PrPC at the α-site, substantially inhibits PrP conversion and prion propagation. Here, we investigated whether stimulation of plasmin activity by acetylsalicylic acid (ASA) would enhance α-cleavage of PrPC and suppression of prion propagation in vitro and in vivo. ASA stimulated plasmin to induce α-cleavage of recombinant PrP, preventing its aggregation, in PrP cleavage and PrP self-aggregation assays. ASA enhanced plasmin-mediated suppression of PrPSc propagation in protein misfolding cyclic amplification. Furthermore, ASA significantly enhanced endogenous plasmin activity, increased C1 fragment generation, and reduced the PrPSc level in both prion-infected cultured cells and mouse brains. These events were translated to the reduction of prion infectivity in standard scrapie cell assay. In addition, ASA prolonged incubation time, prevented disease-associated neuropathology, and attenuated the reduction of synaptic marker proteins in a mouse model of prion disease. Our findings demonstrate that ASA-mediated activation of plasmin promotes α-cleavage of PrPC, hindering prion replication and disease progression in vitro and in vivo. These results suggest that prion suppression is feasible by control of plasmin activity associated with cellular processing of PrPC and propose a potential therapeutic target for prion diseases.
